title: First-Time Eye Drop Instillation

patient.name: Mdm Ho Siew Ling
patient.presenting_complaint: Newly diagnosed glaucoma — here for education on how to use eye drops

history.hpc: Mdm Ho was diagnosed with early primary open-angle glaucoma today during a routine check. The doctor has prescribed latanoprost 0.005% one drop right eye every night. This is the first time she has ever needed to put drops in her own eye. She tells the PSA: 'I tried before when I had pink eye, but I always miss — the drop goes on my cheek, not my eye. My hand shakes a little.' She is anxious about doing it wrong and worried the drop will sting.
history.pmhx: Newly diagnosed POAG right eye. Hypertension on medication. No diabetes. No previous eye surgery.
medications: Latanoprost 0.005% eye drops RE ON — newly prescribed today
history.social_hx: Works long hours at a hawker stall. Lives alone. No family member at home to assist with drops.

examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed at this stage — reviewed by doctor

investigations.note: VA and IOP already completed by clinical staff before this education session.

diagnosis: Patient education session for self-administered eye drop instillation. Mdm Ho has never successfully administered drops to herself. Key challenges: hand tremor, fear of missing the eye, anxiety about stinging. Education goal: patient demonstrates correct technique independently by end of session.

immediate: Explain why the drops are important: 'Latanoprost lowers the pressure in your eye. It is important to use it every night without fail — even when you feel no symptoms — to prevent your glaucoma from getting worse and protect your vision.'
Demonstrate the technique step by step using a clean demo bottle (or capped bottle) first:
Step 1 — Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water
Step 2 — Tilt the head back or lie down — whichever is more comfortable
Step 3 — Use one finger to gently pull the lower eyelid down to form a pocket
Step 4 — Look up and away from the bottle tip
Step 5 — Hold the bottle 1-2 cm above the eye — do not touch the tip to the eye or eyelid
Step 6 — Squeeze gently — one drop is enough
Step 7 — Close the eye gently — do not blink forcefully
Step 8 — Press the inner corner of the eye (nasolacrimal occlusion) for 1-2 minutes to reduce systemic absorption
Have Mdm Ho practise the technique with a saline or demo bottle while you observe
Give specific feedback: 'Good — your head tilt is correct. Try holding the bottle a little closer to your eye.' Do not show frustration if she struggles
For hand tremor: suggest she rest her hand against her cheek or forehead for stability
Explain storage: 'Keep the bottle in the fridge. Once opened, use within 4 weeks.'
Give her the patient information leaflet for latanoprost
follow_up: Confirm she can demonstrate the correct technique before she leaves
If she is still not confident, arrange for a nurse educator to spend more time with her
Advise her to call the clinic if she has any questions about her drops
patient_education: Instil drops at the same time every night — bedtime is ideal for latanoprost (reduces redness side effect during sleep)
If she misses a dose, instil it as soon as she remembers — but if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one; never double up
Latanoprost may cause the eye to look slightly redder and lashes to grow longer over time — this is expected and harmless
Store in the fridge; discard 4 weeks after opening even if there is drop left

key_points: Identifies the patient's specific barrier: hand tremor and previous failed attempts
Confirms the correct eye and correct medication with the patient before the education session
Asks if patient lives alone or has someone to help at home — affects the education plan
Assesses patient's existing knowledge about her condition before educating
Demonstrates the technique correctly step-by-step before asking patient to practise
Observes the patient practise and gives specific, constructive feedback
Offers the practical tip for hand tremor (rest hand against cheek/forehead)
Checks patient's understanding by asking her to explain back the steps
Recognises that patient confidence in technique directly determines medication adherence
Identifies the specific barriers (tremor, missing the eye, anxiety) and addresses each one
Understands that non-adherence to glaucoma drops leads to disease progression and vision loss
Does not rush the session — prioritises patient mastery over clinic efficiency
Uses teach-back method: patient demonstrates the technique, not just listens
Provides written information to reinforce verbal teaching
Covers all key counselling points: timing, storage, duration of use, expected side effects
Escalates to nurse educator if patient is not confident by end of session
